patch.value: The write-time mutation guard and the CI secret gate enforce different rule sets, so content the repository forbids can be made immutable before anything objects

Two secret detectors run in this repository over the same content and enforce different rule sets. The write-time mutation guard flags credential-shaped content before it enters the immutable stream (pm-pim7, extended by pm-fhhhlk for npm and Slack prefixes and by pm-h4zb for GitHub token prefixes). The CI gate scripts/check-secrets.mjs scans tracked files and additionally enforces rules the write-time guard does not have, including absolute-home-path and, since pm-daft, private IP addresses. The consequence is a one-way trap: content the repository forbids can be written, hash-chained and committed, and is then discoverable only after the fact by a gate that runs too late to prevent it.

Demonstrated accidentally on 2026-07-26. A note whose prose contained backticks was passed as a shell argument, so the shell executed the backticked fragments and their error output — carrying absolute host filesystem paths — was persisted into a note_add history entry. The write-time guard accepted it silently. The static gate rejected it on push, and recovery required pm history-redact plus a chain re-anchor, which is the correct remedy but a disproportionate one for content that should never have been accepted.

The asymmetry matters more for history than for source, because a source file can simply be edited while a history entry is immutable by design. Every rule the CI gate enforces but the write-time guard does not is therefore a rule whose violations are permanent by construction and repairable only through an audited rewrite.

The rule inventory is a single declared source consumed by both the write-time mutation guard and the static secret gate, so neither can carry a rule the other lacks; A test fails when the two rule sets diverge, rather than the divergence being discovered by a push that trips the gate; Rules that are deliberately gate-only are declared as such with a recorded reason, so an intentional asymmetry is visible instead of accidental; The guard's advise and block modes apply the full inventory across every mutation surface, matching how the credential rules already behave; Matched values stay redacted in errors, telemetry, and recovery bundles for the newly shared rules exactly as they are for the credential rules; Documentation states which rules block a write and which only fail a build, so an author knows before writing which is which
Make the write-time guard and the repository gate enforce one rule set, so nothing forbidden can become immutable
Violations are refused at the moment of writing instead of discovered after they are hash-chained and pushed
Removes a class of defect whose only remedy is an audited history rewrite, and closes the window where the two detectors disagree
One shared rule inventory consumed by both the mutation guard and the static gate, with drift between them failing a test rather than surfacing as a push failure
The gap was exercised for real this session: a host path reached an immutable stream and required history-redact to remove

value.text:
Live reproduction, 2026-08-03, unplanned. This item predicted the failure and the failure occurred exactly as described, so recording it as evidence rather than as a new finding.

Sequence. I filed pm-9gvazz with a description quoting the workspace absolute path and the harness session-file path, because those two strings ARE the evidence for that defect. The write-time mutation guard accepted the create without objection and the content was hashed into pm-9gvazz's history stream. pm validate reported ok. pm health reported ok. The content was immutable and clean by every check pm itself offers.

The CI secret gate then failed the push: four hits, two in .agents/pm/history/pm-9gvazz.jsonl and two in .agents/pm/issues/pm-9gvazz.toon, all rule absolute-home-path (scripts/check-secrets-lib.mjs). So the repository forbids content that pm had already made permanent - which is the precise statement of this item.

Two details worth keeping, because they sharpen the scope:

First, the ordering is the whole problem. Remediation required pm history-redact, an audited rewrite of an append-only stream, rather than an edit. It worked correctly - two passes, chain re-verified, hash_mismatches_after 0, audit_entry_added true, and the technical content survived - but a write-time refusal would have cost one re-word and no rewrite at all. Every history-redact invocation is a small permanent scar on the immutability claim that a matching write-time rule would have avoided entirely.

Second, the local and hosted halves are already consistent here: node scripts/check-secrets.mjs reproduced all four hits locally with identical output. So this is not a local-versus-hosted parity gap - the parity is fine, and the gap is purely that the rule set lives at commit time and not at mutation time. That distinction matters for the fix: the rules do not need to be re-derived, they need to be shared, and check-secrets-lib.mjs is already a library rather than a script.

Suggested acceptance evidence when this is fixed: creating an item whose body contains an absolute home path must be refused at mutation time with the rule name, and the resulting item must not exist - proven by the secret gate finding nothing afterwards without any redaction having run.
